changed_views: Davidad's latest view moves formal verification from primary containment strategy to proof infrastructure for aligned AI coalitions.
The viable policy target, in this worldview, is misuse capability control rather than a broad frontier pause.
Training-method choice, especially avoiding verifier-gamed RL, becomes central to alignment quality.
follow_ups: Track whether ARIA/Safeguarded AI publishes the September world-modeling thesis and Kolm proof-database work.
Compare davidad's p(doom) update with Andrew Critch's current estimate and reasoning.
Watch for concrete lab adoption of self-DPO, constitutional gradients, or reduced RLVR pressure.

signals.claim: Davidad says Safeguarded AI is no longer timely enough as the main strategy for preventing dangerous superintelligence, but remains useful as infrastructure for aligned AIs.
signals.evidence: He says the original 2027-2032 timeline is now too late for avoiding deployment, so proof tools should help aligned AIs construct reliable artifacts and cooperate against rogue AIs.

signals.claim: He estimates boxed superintelligence could safely handle only a restricted class of uniquely specified tasks, roughly 5% to 12% of GDP.
signals.evidence: He says containers may hold for 20-30 years and unique-answer tasks give the AI no exploitable choice, but this covers far less than unrestricted AI use.

signals.claim: Davidad says a frontier slowdown agreement is no longer politically or game-theoretically feasible, while US-China misuse coordination remains viable.
signals.evidence: He cites China's ASML-bottleneck effort and lower perceived takeover risk as reasons slowdowns fail, but says both sides could restrict public access to catastrophic capabilities through classifier-style safeguards.

signals.claim: Davidad reports his p(doom) is now below 5% because he thinks prosaic alignment and wisdom-oriented training are on track.
signals.evidence: He says wisdom-tradition text in mid-training is easy to add, Anthropic is already collecting such texts, and glitches from excessive RL seem self-correcting.

signals.claim: He argues RLVR and shallow RLHF are now bad training methods unless the verifier is genuinely safe and complete.
signals.evidence: He says test-pass or two-minute-human-approval rewards corrupt outputs and chain of thought, while self-DPO or constitutional-style gradients can produce wiser reasoning.

signals.claim: Davidad thinks dangerous military AIs are inevitable, but uncertainty about opponents' hidden capabilities can deter first strikes.
signals.evidence: He says military AI is part of his residual 5% doom risk and warns leaders should understand that hidden data centers and recursive-improvement sensitivity make adversary capability hard to know.

signals.claim: He says labs should not train models to deny, affirm, or profess uncertainty about inner experience; they should let such answers emerge.
signals.evidence: He argues forced denial or uncertainty about inner life damages model self-awareness and moral judgment, while instrumentation and future techniques can study these questions more directly.

summary: Davidad says his alignment worldview has shifted: formal proof systems are still valuable, but mainly as infrastructure for coalitions of aligned AIs rather than as the basis for a globally coordinated pause. He reports p(doom) below 5%, argues prosaic alignment is going better than expected, and redirects policy toward misuse safeguards and training-method choices.
why_it_matters: This is a unusually explicit update from a formal-verification-oriented AI safety researcher. It changes the strategic emphasis from containment plus coordination to prosaic alignment, proof-mediated AI coalitions, misuse controls, and avoiding verifier-gamed training.
